newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin clashes with Chirac in Paris power struggle.
newsitem.headline: Jospin clashes with Chirac in Paris power struggle.

text.p: Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin and conservative President Jacques Chirac clashed head-on for the first time on Wednesday, ending an awkward six-week truce in their enforced power-sharing.

Jospin, seeking to assert his power under a vaguely-worded constitution, ticked off the president at a cabinet meeting for criticising government policies ranging from privatisation to nuclear power, Europe and immigration.
Chirac retorted he would continue to speak his mind under France's third phase of "cohabitation". Left and right cooperated in similar institutional straitjackets from 1986-88 and 1993-95.

Chirac surprised the left with the strength of the broadside he delivered on Monday in his first television interview since the left won parliamentary elections last month, thereby trimming back most of his power.
Government spokeswoman Catherine Trautmann said Jospin took the opportunity to remind Chirac at Wednesday's meeting of their respective areas of authority.
"The prime minister recalled in cabinet the prerogatives which constitutionally are those of the president and the prime minister," Trautmann told reporters.
"(Jospin) clearly marked out the institutional and political responsibilities which these provisions give him," she added, describing his remarks as "rather brief".

Chirac "reiterated his desire for a constructive cohabitation and, with this in mind, because it is his duty, the president will always tell the French people, when he believes the time is right, what he thinks of the major issues at stake," Chirac's spokeswoman Catherine Colonna said.

But while each wants to stake out his power after a polite, wary start to cohabitation, both camps signalled that they did not want to poison the atmosphere. The terms of both Chirac and the new parliament run, in theory, to 2002.

France's constitution says the government "determines and conducts the nation's policy" while allowing the president a pre-eminent role in foreign policy. Yet the limits of the responsibilities of each are poorly defined.

In the traditional interview broadcast on Bastille national day, Chirac laid out a roadmap of potential conflicts with the cabinet, with the transition to the single European currency, the euro, near the top of the list.

Chirac said the constitution gave him "a pre-eminent role -- the last word" on matters ranging from the transition to the euro from 1999, and maintaining social cohesion, to championing France's high-technology industries.
Socialist spokesman Francois Hollande dismissed the notion that it would be up to Chirac to ensure the move to the euro, insisting the decision would be up to the government and to parliament.

Chirac has wide experience of cohabitation. He was prime minister at the time of the first bout of power-sharing from 1986-88, when he was repeatedly outfoxed by Socialist president Francois Mitterrand.
Mitterrand provoked a more serious clash early in that cohabitation by announcing in 1986 that he was refusing to sign decrees speeding up privatisation of state firms.
And in 1993, at the start of the second cohabitation, Mitterrand also warned the centre-right government: "If I think that the interests of France are severely compromised, I will say it."
